articles.title: England thrash Pakistan inside three days as Joe Root's second era as captain starts with innings win at Headingley
articles.summary: England cruise to 1-0 lead in three-match series versus Pakistan; Joe Root rewarded for funky fields as hosts skittle tourists for 135 in second innings; England can wrap up first series victory since December 2024 by winning second Test at Lord's from Thursday, live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Joe Root won his first Test back as permanent England captain by an innings and 103 runs with Pakistan rolled for 135 before tea on day three at Headingley.

A visiting side demolished for 171 in 48.1 overs on day one were bundled out in 37.3 second time around in Leeds after England made 409 in their sole knock of the match.

Jofra Archer (3-50), much improved from a rusty first-innings effort, struck twice early on to reduce Pakistan to 13-2 and Josh Tongue's (3-43) three-wicket burst post-lunch, including that of Shan Masood (29), pretty much ended any hope of the tourists reaching day four.

  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract
  • Scorecard: England vs Pakistan, first Test, Headingley
  • England vs Pakistan - as it happened on day three in Leeds

Root was rewarded for some funky fields - Azan Awais (9) clipped Archer to him at leg slip, Saud Shakeel (14) picked out Dan Lawrence in an unorthodox backward square spot off Tongue - as his team crushed their inexperienced opponents in a one-sided contest.

Gus Atkinson (1-11) cleaned up a swiping top-scorer Mohammad Rizwan (41) to put England on the brink before Mohammad Abbas (6) ballooned Archer to Lawrence to end a game in which Ollie Robinson (3-29) and Tongue bagged eight wickets each.

England are now toasting just a third win in their last 11 Tests and if they triumph in the second fixture at Lord's from Thursday - 11am first ball, live on Sky Sports - they will secure a first series victory since a 2-1 success in New Zealand in December 2024.

They did thrash Zimbabwe in a one-off game at Trent Bridge last summer but have lost two and drawn one of their last three multi-match contests, with a 2-2 stalemate against India preceding a 4-1 drubbing in Australia and 2-1 home defeat to New Zealand.

Bigger challenges to come but Root starts well

Stiffer tests of Root's captaincy are still to come.

Hopefully in this three-match assignment, although Pakistan's lack of quality and x-factor could scupper that, but certainly in South Africa over the winter - new permanent head coach Stephen Fleming's first series in charge - and next summer's Ashes.

Yet this was an encouraging start, with England's run-rate of 4.55 an over owing more to Pakistan's wayward bowling and sloppy fielding than Bazball-style batting, with Harry Brook showing welcome restraint during a 93-ball 91 on his home ground..

First-innings five-fors for Robinson and Tongue, England's relentlessness with the ball, and half-centuries from Root and Brook as well as the recalled Lawrence and Jordan Cox were big ticks.

Jamie Smith's dismissal - hacking an innocuous short ball from Khurram Shahzad (3-133) to midwicket to fall for 25 after England began day three on 366-8, leading by 195 - a lowlight.

Around Smith's exit, Archer (23no) and Tongue (8) struck some glittering boundaries - Archer smoking the game's sole six, off Khurram.

Pakistan crumble again with the bat amid England onslaught

Archer then got stuck into Pakistan's openers, forcing a swaying Imam to glove through to Smith and then extracting Azan, after the latter had avoided the indignity of a pair having been lbw to Robinson from the first ball of the match.

Abdullah Shafique (15) and Masood steadied Pakistan for a spell, only for the former to prod limply at a Robinson delivery and edge to Brook at second slip shortly before lunch.

Tongue vaporised Saud, Masood and stand-in skipper Salman Ali Agha (4) - deputising for the injured Babar Azam (hand) - when the action restarted, with Masood caught at slip and Salman lbw to a nip-backer in the same over.

When Ali Usman (7) - whose five-wicket haul was one of the few bright sparks for Pakistan over a chastening three days - fell to an excellent diving slip catch from Cox, after the ball had ballooned up off Smith's thigh, the tourists were toast.

Pakistan were then eight down when Rizwan bizarrely exposed tailender Khurram (8) to Robinson just one ball into an over and the No 9 duly nicked off - one of many blunders Salman's men made in Yorkshire.

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Nasser Hussain praises 'maturity' in Joe Root's return as captain after dominant three-day win at Headingley
articles.summary: Nasser Hussain praised Joe Root’s “maturity” after England’s win over Pakistan at Headingley, while Stuart Broad hailed Josh Tongue as “England’s best bowler”; watch the second Test at Lord’s live on Sky Sports Cricket from 10am Thursday
articles.body:
Nasser Hussain praised Joe Root’s poised return to the captaincy after England secured a thumping three-day victory over Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs in the first Test at Headingley.

The skipper oversaw a dominant all-round performance, with Josh Tongue (8-89) and Ollie Robinson (8-80) leading the way with the ball, while vice-captain Harry Brook (91), Jordan Cox (73) and Root himself (66) helped England to 409 in their only innings.

Hussain recognised the difference in approach to his last spell as captain between 2017 and 2022, praising a reinvigorated Root's return to the helm:

  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream England vs Pakistan no contract
  • Scorecard: England vs Pakistan, first Test, Headingley
  • As it happened: England vs Pakistan, day three

"The biggest thing [about this Test match] was Joe Root," Hussain said on Sky Sports Cricket.

"He said to Michael Atherton in an interview: 'judge me not on how I was last time, but how I am now.'

"If you'd just come down and seen Joe this week, these three days, albeit against a poor Pakistan side, you'll say he had a really good three days as captain.

"The decision with the balance of the side [worked out], electing not to have a frontline spinner. I know some of that was enforced because of no Ben Stokes - and we'll come on to that - but it was also the toss decision, and then the way he batted, and then the way he captained in the field.

"It was never I'm trying to be Stokes. It was just Joe Root being Joe. He had a smile on his face.

"Compare that to [the second Test against New Zealand] at The Oval, where he was handed a hospital pass [by being made interim captain]. He looked a bit dishevelled by the end of that, to be honest, and he didn't have his best game as captain there.

But I think he was really good here. And that's a positive sign."

Nasser: New maturity about Root's England

Hussain also highlighted a change in approach from Root's predecessor, Stokes, who had previously been criticised for a lack of attention to detail, saying England showed a new "maturity" alongside vice-captain Brook in their dominant victory.

"I thought there was a maturity about their performance here on and off the field as well. Just listening to Harry Brook and the interview he gave me this morning, you just sensed some more mature answers - saying 'we have had a look at ourselves'.

"It's not [the Bazball attitude] of 'this is the only way we play and you lot don't like it - We don't care.'

"It was realising that there are a lot of good bits [to McCullum and Stokes], as Joe said to Michael Atherton, to take forward.

"I thought they got the tempo of batting right, albeit because they were given a full ball every over.

"So I sense there's a bit more of a maturity to their performance."

Broad: Tongue is England's best bowler

Stuart Broad also praised the performance of Tongue after his eight-wicket haul, saying the bowler has established himself as one of England's most valuable players:

"I think he's England's best bowler," Broad said on Sky Sports.

"He's England's trump card really at the moment. The most valuable bowler that England have.

"He looks fit, he looks like he's bowling a good amount of overs, keeping his bowling maintenance rather than stopping and starting the whole time because he's had injury problems, right?

"That's been his thing that stopped him over the last six, seven years. So he'll want to continue that sort of form by bowling, staying fit. He looks fit and he holds the key for England to be successful over the next year."

articles.title: Joe Root hails England's bowlers after statement Pakistan win, and reveals he has been in contact with Stephen Fleming every day
articles.summary: Joe Root stressed the importance of England's dominant win against Pakistan, and hailed his bowlers, after the hosts secured victory by an innings and 103 runs at Headingley; watch the second Test live on Sky Sports Cricket from 10am on Thursday
articles.body:
Joe Root was thrilled by the performances of his bowlers as England's pace attack dismissed Pakistan for 135 before tea, to seal a statement three-day victory in the first Test at Headingley.

Pakistan were bowled out for 171 in 48.1 overs on day one, with England responding with an insuperable 409, as they romped their way to victory by an innings and 103 runs, in what was a dream start for Root in his second spell as captain.

On day three, Ollie Robinson (3-29), Jofra Archer (3-50) and Josh Tongue (3-43) seized full advantage of a worn Headingley pitch as they took three wickets apiece, while Gus Atkinson (1-11) followed up with a wicket of his own.

  • England romp to three-day win vs Pakistan
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract
  • Scorecard: England vs Pakistan, first Test, Headingley
  • England vs Pakistan - as it happened on day three in Leeds

Root hailed his bowlers after the victory, claiming they "don't know just how good they can be".

"I don't think our bowlers understand well that they complement each other in these conditions, and what they're capable of doing," the Yorkshireman said.

"It's really nice for them to see that and to start the series like that."

Archer, who went wicketless in Pakistan's first innings, got England off to a flying start, dismissing both Pakistan openers, Azan Awais and Imam-ul-Haq inside four overs.

Tongue and Robinson were prolific throughout the match, with both completing eight-wicket hauls.

Robinson, the pick of the bowlers, has now won man-of-the-match awards in the two Tests he has played this summer, and Root hailed the 32-year-old for his ability to keep threatening Pakistan's batters late into the match.

"I thought Robinson was brilliant," Root said.

"The fact that he's still as effective in the second innings, having bowled 18 overs, and his understanding of what his requirements are in different phases of the game is important.

"For him to be effective as the pitch changed throughout and to consistently keep asking difficult questions is a really good sign for us."

'It's always important to win a Test match'

After a chaotic few months, following the departures of former captain Ben Stokes and head coach Brendon McCullum, Root, who was trapped lbw for 66 on day two, stressed the importance of the victory.

But he added England were eager to "not get too carried away".

"It's always important to win a Test match," Root said.

"You're playing for England, right? It's what you set out to do every time you walk out on to that field.

"It's more the fact that we delivered on everything we spoke about, that's the most pleasing thing and the most enjoyable thing about all of it.

"There's also an understanding that this is one game; there's going to be other challenges and different things to manage. That's the exciting part, and it's taking the confidence from this and being skilful to deal with that next thing, which will be Lord's."

After returning to captain England following a four-year hiatus, Root said things were different this time around.

"It was quite easy on occasion to leave Jimmy Anderson and Stuart Broad to it," Root said, reflecting on his previous spell as captain. "Very experienced, they knew how they were going to operate.

"There's a lot of different things this time round.

"I'm very different as well. With everything going on around the Test match it was important to give as much clarity and simplicity to what we were trying to achieve and we delivered on that brilliantly."

Root in contact with Fleming every day

Root also revealed incumbent England head coach Stephen Fleming has been in contact with him "every day".

Fleming will not take up the new role until after England's three-match series against Pakistan.

"He's kept tabs on things," Root said.

"It's just been great to have him on the end of the phone and I can speak to him as much or as little as I like.

"It's great that he's very invested already in what we're trying to achieve and there's been constant communication with Marcus Trescothick and me."

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Robinson, Tongue & Cox give hosts hope for brighter future
articles.summary: Have England improved or were Pakistan really poor? BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt analyses the first-Test talking points from Headingley.
articles.body:
England's crushing victory over Pakistan was the ideal start to Joe Root's second reign as Test captain.

The home side could not have wished for a more straightforward beginning to a new era as they look to move on from the chaos of the past year.

England's innings win comes with the context of a desperate performance from Pakistan, so any judgements on progress should be reserved for now.

Still, Headingley taught us some things. Here are the takeaways.

England are rebuilding their bowling attack for two reasons.

First, the retirement of Ben Stokes has robbed them not only of inspiration, but of balance.

Secondly, Stokes has followed Stuart Broad, James Anderson, Chris Woakes and, most likely, Mark Wood out of the door. That is 1,871 Test wickets lost in less than three years.

The first stab at a post-Stokes team included four frontline seamers â Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson â supported by the part-time off-breaks of Dan Lawrence.

In helpful conditions, it could not have gone better for England. Robinson and Tongue took eight wickets apiece, while Archer and Atkinson improved after a rusty first innings when they struggled to adapt following a month playing in The Hundred. Lawrence bowled only one over in the match.

Clearly, there will be times when England need a frontline spinner, but there is no consistently Test-class spinner in the country right now.

There is an argument to be made that England should continue to stack their attack with seamers because they are the best bowlers â Root said they "don't know how good they could be".

The likes of Sam Cook and Brydon Carse wait in the wings to step in or provide different skills if necessary, meaning England have a large squad of pacemen to choose from.

A trip to Bangladesh in February will mean England have to find some spin. For now, they should stay in the fast lane.

'Plug him in as attack leader' - England-Pakistan player ratings Published 4 days ago

'Plug him in as attack leader' - England-Pakistan player ratings

It would be 'nice to have choice' over Ashes venues - Root Published 3 days ago

It would be 'nice to have choice' over Ashes venues - Root

Jordan Cox has waited a long time for a proper opportunity in Test cricket. Now that it has finally arrived, the Essex batter looks at home at the highest level.

Deputising for the injured Jacob Bethell at number three, Cox impressed with an assured 73. He showed patience and sound judgement, though still had the range of strokes to push the scoring along at a healthy rate without taking risks.

Admittedly, the Pakistan attack Cox faced was far from the most fearsome in Test cricket. None of their seamers had the pace to test his ticker against the short ball.

But, occasionally, players come along and appear instantly suited to Test cricket. Cox seems to fit into that bracket.

His blemish was missing out on the really big score that would have made it impossible for the selectors to leave him out when Bethell returns. Cox potentially has four more innings in this series to make himself undroppable.

If the 25-year-old does demand a place in the XI for the December tour of South Africa and beyond, it leaves England with a dilemma.

Is opener Emilio Gay vulnerable? Bethell is now England's opener in one-day cricket, while Cox opened for Kent at the beginning of his first-class career.

Cox can also keep wicket. Might he put pressure on Jamie Smith? Speaking of whomâ¦

Smith was one of the players who most noticeably wilted under the pressure and scrutiny of the Ashes tour.

He was not helped by a lack of attention to his wicketkeeping in training. Whether it was because a threadbare backroom team was overworked, or England's overall attitude was not good enough, Smith was rarely seen doing the hard yards with the gloves on.

There has been a change this summer. Since joining the coaching staff, former England women's wicketkeeper Sarah Taylor has worked closely with Smith, who has also been able to do more wicketkeeping training with his county Surrey since recovering from a finger injury.

Another circumstance was an injury to Surrey's regular keeper Ben Foakes, one of the best glovemen in the world. It gave Smith three consecutive games behind the stumps in the County Championship in the early part of the season.

The result has been a definite improvement in Smith's keeping for England. It's not as if the 26-year-old ever looked out of place behind the stumps in Test cricket, but he has shown off a greater range of skills this summer, particularly standing up to the fast-medium of Robinson.

At one point, in the third Test against New Zealand at Trent Bridge, Smith even stood up to the pacey Archer.

Not all progress is linear. Smith's Test batting average has dipped below 40 and he needs to avoid developing a habit for maddening modes of dismissal.

The man who somehow got out to a Marnus Labuschagne bouncer in Sydney tamely holed out for 25 on Friday morning when there was an opportunity for a much bigger contribution.

If Cox or Lawrence fill their batting boots this summer, then England's top-order will become congested. Smith must ensure he does not become vulnerable.

Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, is not here. Brendon McCullum's replacement is not due to arrive in the UK until September, by which time the Pakistan series could be over.

Fleming was appointed last month, yet will not take charge of England in a Test until South Africa at Christmas.

The delay has not fully been explained, apart from perhaps a desire to give Fleming a break after almost two decades with Chennai Super Kings.

You will have your own opinions on that one. Being in charge of an Indian Premier League team is intense, but CSK's last match was on 21 May, seven months before England's first Test against the Proteas. Could Fleming, now with one of the biggest jobs in coaching, not have been part of a month-long series against Pakistan?

Either way, Root revealed the New Zealander had been in daily contact during the Headingley Test. "It's been great to have him on the end of the phone," said the captain.

Fleming's influence is not immediately obvious, simply because England were not tested in Leeds.

Should things get more difficult in the remaining two Tests, or if a crucial selection decision needs to be made, perhaps vital input will come from the Flemphone.

'I fear for them' - pundits lament 'desperate times' for Pakistan Published 4 days ago

'I fear for them' - pundits lament 'desperate times' for Pakistan

A win is a win for England, much needed after only two in their previous 10. However, they should have been better than two wins in 10, and the dismal nature of Pakistan's performance means Root's men can only take limited encouragement from their week in Leeds.

Nothing went right for Pakistan, from the moment captain Babar Azam was ruled out with a thumb injury. Their batting was brittle, their bowling scattergun and their fielding shoddy.

Babar's team beat West Indies in Trinidad earlier this month to earn a 1-1 series draw, yet that was Pakistan's first Test win away from home in more than three years.

They are heavily reliant on winning Tests on spinning pitches, which is why they switched to worn tracks on England's last visit to Pakistan in 2024. When pace bowling becomes the dominant weapon, Pakistan have neither the bowlers nor batters to thrive in the conditions.

Now they head to Lord's, where not one over of spin was bowled in England's shootout win over New Zealand in June.

The surface at the home of cricket could be much different this time around, or a sporty pitch could act as a leveller between the two teams.

Still, the smart money is on another England victory to complete their first series win against anyone in almost two years.

articles.title: England player ratings: Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue take top marks after three-day victory over Pakistan in first Test
articles.summary: Joe Root was excellent on his return to the captaincy while Harry Brook batted with maturity and Jordan Cox looked the part after replacing the injured Jacob Bethell at No 3; watch second Test, at Lord's, live on Sky Sports Cricket from 10am on Thursday (11am first ball)
articles.body:
We rate England's players after the thumping innings win over Pakistan at Headingley as Joe Root's side took a 1-0 lead in the three-match Test series...

Ben Duckett - 4

15 off 28 balls

Duckett suffers here from the fact Pakistan did not make England bat again, leaving him unable to add to his score with a second knock after a 28-ball 15 first time around.

  • England romp to three-day win on Joe Root's captaincy return
  • Scorecard: England vs Pakistan, first Test, Headingley
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract

The opener - who has rediscovered his mojo following a tough Ashes, impressing against New Zealand and in The Hundred - will hope to play a more central role in the Tests at Lord's and Edgbaston.

Emilio Gay - 6

33 from 31 balls

Gay came into this game off the back of a pair in a warm-up match so nerves would have been fluttering - but he eased those with a number of sweetly-struck boundaries before nicking off shortly after Duckett's dismissal.

The Durham man does look vulnerable to balls angled across him yet has shown plenty of promise early in his Test career, with two fifties versus New Zealand. Will hope for a big knock soon.

Jordan Cox - 8.5

73 from 100 balls

He may only be keeping the No 3 spot warm until Jacob Bethell (knee) is fit again but Cox put in a good case to stay in the XI long term with an authoritative half-century at first drop. He was aided by some poor Pakistan bowling but still looked the part.

It may be that Cox's best route into the XI going forward is as wicketkeeper-batter so an impressive next two Tests as well and he could pressure Jamie Smith for that post.

He took two catches at slip on the third and final day in Leeds, including a superb diving effort after the ball had ballooned up off gloveman Smith's thigh.

Joe Root - 9

66 from 112 balls

Almost everything Root touched in this Test, on his return to the permanent captaincy, turned to gold, bar his limp shot and even worse review on the second day.

He had batted with his usual brilliance before that and was excellent as captain, having had the fortune of winning the toss and inserting Pakistan under leaden skies.

Root, who largely stood at mid-off to have the ear of his bowlers, showed a ruthless streak by hooking Jofra Archer after two underwhelming overs in the first innings.

His funky field placings, including deploying himself at leg slip at one point, also paid off as England secured just a third win in their last 11 Tests. A fine start to the new era.

Harry Brook - 9

91 from 93 balls

If fears over maturity was a reason Brook was overlooked when it came to deciding Ben Stokes' successor as Test skipper, then the vice-captain showed signs of growth in Leeds, with his near-run-a-ball 91 enterprising, of course, but not reckless.

Brook told Sky Sports the morning after that the Headingley pitch meant he did not need to play any "rash shots", something he has been guilty of in the past.

The Yorkshireman could have been caught at slip on one - and if he had questions over his temperament would probably have arisen again - but he made Pakistan pay before heartbreakingly falling in the 90s in a Test on home turf for the second year running.

Dan Lawrence - 8

51 from 79 balls
0-0 from one over in second innings

Lawrence had the unenviable - and impossible - task of replacing Stokes in the XI. His part-time spin bowling was only used for one over with the game moving so quickly but his batting starred as he struck nine fours in his fifty, around the odd jittery moment.

A bigger role with the ball may come if Pakistan improve. Only then will we probably know if Lawrence is the right fit in the post-Stokes era or more tinkering is needed.

Sam Curran's injury means Lawrence will probably see out the summer at least.

Jamie Smith - 6

25 off 42 balls

Smith was faultless behind the stumps but will be annoyed by his avoidable dismissal, ballooning a short ball tamely to midwicket. That said, he was left with the tail and his exit did not make any difference to the result.

If he can get back to scoring the regular runs someone of his talent should and maintain his Headingley standards with the gloves, then there will be no questioning his place.

It not, and Cox continues to flourish, then England could have a big decision to make when Bethell is fit again.

Gus Atkinson - 5

0-40 from 12 overs in first innings
1-11 from eight overs in second innings

Much like fellow seamer Archer, Atkinson looked a little rusty in the first innings. Understandable perhaps considering he had just come off a long run of white-ball cricket - a bit for England and lot for Hundred champions Manchester Super Giants.

And much like Archer, he was better in the second innings, bagging his sole wicket of the game when he cleaned up Mohammad Rizwan to put his side on the brink.

This was a new role for Atkinson to what he has been accustomed to of late, moving from new-ball man to first change as Archer and Ollie Robinson shared the fresh Dukes.

Ollie Robinson - 10

5-51 from 18 overs in first innings
3-29 from 11 overs in second innings

Simply irresistible. Worries over Robinson's durability may remain - this was his first Test since the opening game of the summer against New Zealand having suffered a niggle - but there is no doubting his skill and control. He has the ball on a string.

The Sussex seamer pinned Azan Awais lbw to the first ball of the match and was a constant menace with his probing line and length and subtle variations and seam movement. He was helped by conditions and a fragile batting line-up but that's taking nothing away from him.

Now, though, he needs to stay fit.

Jofra Archer - 7

23no from 25 balls
0-26 from nine overs in first innings
3-50 from 10.3 overs in second innings

Archer lacked rhythm and was a bit too leg-side in the first innings. However, he got back in the red-ball groove on day three, bowling with a big smile and real snap.

He made light work of Pakistan openers Imam-ul-Haq and Azan to reduce the tourists to 13-2 before picking up the match-clinching wicket of Mohammad Abbas.

Archer will also be pleased with his batting - he struck the game's sole six and added two fours as well to help England take their first-innings lead in excess of 200.

Josh Tongue - 10

5-46 from 9.1 overs in first innings
3-43 from seven overs in second innings

We had the peculiar sight of the ball being cut in half and Tongue and Robinson taking a segment each after their first-innings five-fors and when they both ended up with eight wickets in the Test, it must have made picking player of the match a tough ask.

Robinson took that accolade but we can't split the seamers in our ratings - each get 10 out of 10.

Tongue built on Robinson's early work in Pakistan's first dig, nipping in to break a 91-run third-wicket stand and then scything through the lower middle order, while his three wickets soon after lunch on the third day largely guaranteed we would not have a fourth.

Hailed as England's "best and most valuable bowler" and "a real trump card" by Sky Sports' Stuart Broad, Tongue will have a massive role to play moving forward. He shone in the last Ashes and his success in the next one, in 2027, could be crucial.

paragraphs:
We rate England's players after the thumping innings win over Pakistan at Headingley as Joe Root's side took a 1-0 lead in the three-match Test series...

Ben Duckett - 4

15 off 28 balls

Duckett suffers here from the fact Pakistan did not make England bat again, leaving him unable to add to his score with a second knock after a 28-ball 15 first time around.

  • England romp to three-day win on Joe Root's captaincy return
  • Scorecard: England vs Pakistan, first Test, Headingley
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract

The opener - who has rediscovered his mojo following a tough Ashes, impressing against New Zealand and in The Hundred - will hope to play a more central role in the Tests at Lord's and Edgbaston.

Emilio Gay - 6

33 from 31 balls

Gay came into this game off the back of a pair in a warm-up match so nerves would have been fluttering - but he eased those with a number of sweetly-struck boundaries before nicking off shortly after Duckett's dismissal.

The Durham man does look vulnerable to balls angled across him yet has shown plenty of promise early in his Test career, with two fifties versus New Zealand. Will hope for a big knock soon.

Jordan Cox - 8.5

73 from 100 balls

He may only be keeping the No 3 spot warm until Jacob Bethell (knee) is fit again but Cox put in a good case to stay in the XI long term with an authoritative half-century at first drop. He was aided by some poor Pakistan bowling but still looked the part.

It may be that Cox's best route into the XI going forward is as wicketkeeper-batter so an impressive next two Tests as well and he could pressure Jamie Smith for that post.

He took two catches at slip on the third and final day in Leeds, including a superb diving effort after the ball had ballooned up off gloveman Smith's thigh.

Joe Root - 9

66 from 112 balls

Almost everything Root touched in this Test, on his return to the permanent captaincy, turned to gold, bar his limp shot and even worse review on the second day.

He had batted with his usual brilliance before that and was excellent as captain, having had the fortune of winning the toss and inserting Pakistan under leaden skies.

Root, who largely stood at mid-off to have the ear of his bowlers, showed a ruthless streak by hooking Jofra Archer after two underwhelming overs in the first innings.

His funky field placings, including deploying himself at leg slip at one point, also paid off as England secured just a third win in their last 11 Tests. A fine start to the new era.

Harry Brook - 9

91 from 93 balls

If fears over maturity was a reason Brook was overlooked when it came to deciding Ben Stokes' successor as Test skipper, then the vice-captain showed signs of growth in Leeds, with his near-run-a-ball 91 enterprising, of course, but not reckless.

Brook told Sky Sports the morning after that the Headingley pitch meant he did not need to play any "rash shots", something he has been guilty of in the past.

The Yorkshireman could have been caught at slip on one - and if he had questions over his temperament would probably have arisen again - but he made Pakistan pay before heartbreakingly falling in the 90s in a Test on home turf for the second year running.

Dan Lawrence - 8

51 from 79 balls
0-0 from one over in second innings

Lawrence had the unenviable - and impossible - task of replacing Stokes in the XI. His part-time spin bowling was only used for one over with the game moving so quickly but his batting starred as he struck nine fours in his fifty, around the odd jittery moment.

A bigger role with the ball may come if Pakistan improve. Only then will we probably know if Lawrence is the right fit in the post-Stokes era or more tinkering is needed.

Sam Curran's injury means Lawrence will probably see out the summer at least.

Jamie Smith - 6

25 off 42 balls

Smith was faultless behind the stumps but will be annoyed by his avoidable dismissal, ballooning a short ball tamely to midwicket. That said, he was left with the tail and his exit did not make any difference to the result.

If he can get back to scoring the regular runs someone of his talent should and maintain his Headingley standards with the gloves, then there will be no questioning his place.

It not, and Cox continues to flourish, then England could have a big decision to make when Bethell is fit again.

Gus Atkinson - 5

0-40 from 12 overs in first innings
1-11 from eight overs in second innings

Much like fellow seamer Archer, Atkinson looked a little rusty in the first innings. Understandable perhaps considering he had just come off a long run of white-ball cricket - a bit for England and lot for Hundred champions Manchester Super Giants.

articles.title: Ben Stokes blasts 'shambolic' decision to leave Headingley off 2027 men's Ashes schedule
articles.summary: Ben Stokes has criticised the decision to stage the 2027 men's Ashes without a single Test in the north of England; the former England captain reacted on his Instagram story after Joe Root, Harry Brook and Mark Butcher had questioned the schedule
articles.body:
Ben Stokes has described the decision to leave Headingley off the schedule for the 2027 men's Ashes as "shambolic".

The lack of a northern venue as part of the men's Ashes schedule has come under scrutiny from players, pundits and fans since it was announced.

Former England captain Stokes delivered his verdict on Instagram in response to a post about the schedule, before adding "Great win though" in a nod to England's innings-and-103 run demolition of Pakistan at the Leeds ground this week.

  • The Ashes: Full 2027 schedule and venues
  • Latest cricket scorecards and results
  • Listen to the Sky Sports Cricket podcast

Joe Root, the man who replaced Stokes as captain, described Headingley's absence as a "shame", and pointed to England's strong record at the venue.

"Shame is an understatement [to be honest]," said Stokes in response. "Shambolic would be more appropriate."

No venue carries more Stokes history. It was at Headingley in 2019 that his famous unbeaten 135 dragged England to a record chase of 359, sharing an unbroken last-wicket stand of 76 with Jack Leach to keep that Ashes series alive in one of the greatest finishes the game has seen.

Next summer's series will be played across five grounds, with the opening Test in Nottingham the most northerly fixture.

Lord's, Edgbaston and The Kia Oval all return, Southampton's Utilita Bowl will stage a men's Ashes Test for the first time, and Headingley and Old Trafford – home to so many of the series' most storied days – are nowhere on the roster.

England's recent record only strengthens the case, with the men's team currently on a streak of seven consecutive Test wins at Headingley, the latest completed inside three days this week.

Former England batter Mark Butcher, who scored a century at Headingley in the Ashes 25 years ago, questioned the logic of the ECB's decision making on Sky Sports.

"I find it extraordinary that there'll be no Ashes cricket up in the north of England beyond Trent Bridge next year. It's bizarre," he said.

"Whether that's here at Headingley or whether it's at Old Trafford, that's a point for the bean counters to decide, or whoever's turn that might be.

"The game being marketed as a game for everybody needs to have some representation and needs to have a game in the north."

Harry Brook, speaking at Headingley during the Pakistan Test, invoked his former captain's finest hour when asked how disappointed he was by the omission.

"Slightly, to be honest. I think we've had a hell of a lot of success here in Test match cricket," he said. "You go back to 2019 in the Ashes when Stokesy played that ridiculous innings, then the last Ashes Test match a couple of years ago where we kept the Ashes alive.

"I personally love playing here. It's one of my favourites, if not my favourite ground to bat on. It is disappointing, but we don't make those decisions. The hierarchy make them and we just get told where to play."

Men's Ashes series in England 2027

All times UK and Ireland

First Test: Friday June 18 - Tuesday June 22 (11am) - Trent Bridge, Nottingham

Second Test: Wednesday June 30 - Sunday July 4 (11am) - Lord's

Third Test: Thursday July 8 - Monday July 12 (11am) - Edgbaston, Birmingham

Fourth Test: Wednesday July 21 - Sunday July 25 (11am) - Utilita Bowl, Southampton

Fifth Test: Thursday July 29 - Monday August 2 (11am) - The Kia Oval, London

articles.title: England vs Pakistan: Joe Root's captaincy and Harry Brook's maturity promising for hosts in first Test as tourists outclassed
articles.summary: England's thumping win at Headingley a positive start to new era but caveated by how bad Pakistan were with bat, ball and in the field; it remains unclear how Joe Root's side should replace Ben Stokes long term - and how on earth tourists can get back in three-match series
articles.body:
Joe Root's return match as England Test captain could hardly have gone better - a three-day win and a weekend off.

The fact that fast bowler Josh Tongue had the opportunity to focus on his beloved Manchester United's Saturday-lunchtime Premier League opener against Hull City owed much to England's excellence but more so Pakistan's ineptitude.

A game that started on Wednesday was done before tea on Friday. Had rain not fallen across the first two days, it could conceivably have concluded on Thursday evening.

  • England romp to three-day win on Joe Root's captaincy return
  • England player ratings: Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue star
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract

As a result, there are similarities between this England reset and the one they had at the start of the summer against New Zealand at Lord's, in that the speed of the game rendered it hard to assess how much progress had actually been made.

Against the Black Caps in June, in the last knockings of Bazball, the poor pitch was chiefly to blame for the Test lasting only 166 overs. At Headingley this week, Pakistan's lack of quality was a key factor in the game being over in 175.3.

This Leeds deck was a good one. It was how Pakistan batted and bowled on in that was the problem, allied with how they fielded. The tourists had a shocker on all three fronts.

That has to be a caveat when it comes to assessing England but Pakistan's myriad issues should not entirely detract from a fine performance from the home side.

What did we learn from England in Leeds?

While too early to make sweeping calls about this new England - the permanent coach, Stephen Fleming, is not even in the country yet, although did chat to Root on the phone during the Headingley Test - there were a few learnings. Root's captaincy for one.

The Yorkshireman had been left broken at the end of his first stint in the role, as the losses totted up and he had to navigate Covid bubbles, but he looked refreshed and revitalised on his home ground as he chalked up a record-extending 28th win in charge.

Switching from slip to mid-off allowed him to be closer to his bowlers, while a switch from mid-off to leg slip at one point paid off as he caught Azan Awais off Jofra Archer.

We also saw a ruthless streak when Root withdrew Archer from the attack on day one after two unimpactful overs with the new ball. There was much to admire as Root made tactical tweaks but did not try to lead like predecessor Ben Stokes.

We also saw a maturity in Harry Brook's batting with the vice-captain parking the dancing down the wicket and the falling-over scoops to play in a more orthodox, restrained manner. There was no need for any "rash shots", he later told Sky Sports.

Brook simply waited for Pakistan to bowl a bad ball - and, boy, did they bowl lots of those - rather than attempt to force the issue. If he can mix that measured approach with his breath-taking talent going forward, there is no limit on what he could achieve.

England were assured with the bat as a whole. No Bazball going on here. Just positive, clinical strokeplay, against an admittedly powderpuff and profligate attack.

We discovered that England have depth in their middle-order batting with Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence scoring sprightly half-centuries after replacing Jacob Bethell (injured) and Stokes (retired) in the side - Cox, especially, looks at home at this level.

Unfortunately, Pakistan wilting twice means we did not learn whether having Lawrence as the main spin option around a four-pronged pace attack is the way England should look to replace Stokes long term. Lawrence only bowled one over in the game.

The success of the pace quartet - Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue, Archer and Gus Atkinson - makes it unlikely a frontline spinner will be picked for the second Test.

Plus, would selecting one actually weaken England in that their best bowlers are their quicks? A spinner would improve the over rate, for sure, but perhaps not much else.

Poor Pakistan look set for long series

What we learned most of all, though, is that this Pakistan side is not very good.

Yes, they were missing captain and best batter Babar Azam due to a hand injury and had the misfortune of losing the toss to be stuck in on day one under leaden skies.

And, yes, this is Pakistan so a rousing comeback from nowhere should not be completely discounted. They have done it plenty of times in the past.

But that feels fanciful right now with the batting line-up not accustomed to English conditions, the bowling attack lacking venom and the fielding at Headingley appalling.

The lack of Pakistan fans in the ground was also extremely disappointing and probably speaks volumes for the connection they have with this team at the moment.

It could be a long series for Pakistan - and a very short one in terms of how many days of cricket we actually see. England winning well inside the distance at Lord's and Edgbaston appears the likely outcome here, provided the rain holds off.

Babar's return will bolster the batting but there is no mystery or express pace to the bowling, traits that Pakistan have been famous for producing in the past, through Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis, Shoaib Akhtar, Saeed Ajmal, Abdul Qadir et al. It's all too samey.

Resets have been England's thing of late. Maybe it is time for Pakistan to undergo one, having lost 14 of their last 19 Tests.

Everyone loves a weekend off, although you suspect Pakistan won't be enjoying theirs, after a match that could hardly have gone worse.

articles.title: Former England captain Ben Stokes stars as Durham thump Derbyshire to lift Rothesay County Championship promotion hopes
articles.summary: Ex-England skipper Ben Stokes stars as Durham thump Derbyshire to lift Championship promotion hopes while Division One leaders Nottinghamshire wrapped up a 145-run win against Surrey; Warwickshire climb up to second
articles.body:
Ben Stokes starred again with bat and ball as Durham boosted their Rothesay County Championship promotion hopes with a crushing 338-run win at Derbyshire with a day to spare.

The former England captain followed up his half-century and two wickets in the first innings by making an unbeaten 66 before taking 5-17 as Derbyshire were skittled out for 84 while chasing an unlikely 423 for victory.

After resuming their first innings on 127-6, trailing by 156, Derbyshire were all out for 156, with Durham's Matthew Potts finishing with 5-46.

  • County Championship scorecards
  • Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW

Durham opener Ben McKinney then made a brilliant 140 off 162 deliveries and Will Rhodes made 52 before a 55-ball 66 not out from Stokes saw the visitors declare on 295-6.

Stokes then took three wickets in four balls as Derbyshire's second innings capitulated, with Potts chipping in with 3-22.

Division One leaders Nottinghamshire wrapped up a 145-run win against Surrey at The Oval despite Ollie Pope's 111 for the hosts, who were all out for 183 in their second innings.

Nottinghamshire's Olly Stone and Dillon Pennington shared seven wickets between them after Joe Clarke's 95 helped the visitors to 306 all out after they had resumed on 147-3.

Warwickshire completed a thrilling one-wicket win against Sussex at Edgbaston to climb up to second in Division One.

Chris Woakes edged the winning boundary after Warwickshire had slipped from 149-3 to 202-9 as they chased 203 for victory after restricting Sussex to 207 in their second innings.

Essex batter Charlie Allison made 105 not out at Taunton to lift his side to 314 for three after they had followed on against third-placed Somerset, to lead by three runs with seven wickets remaining.

Gloucestershire pair Ollie Price (63 not out) and James Bracey (45 not out) helped their side reach 248-3 in Cheltenham and they lead Worcestershire by 131 runs with seven wickets in hand.

Northamptonshire opener Ricardo Vasconcelos made 100 to put his side in control at Old Trafford against Lancashire.

The visitors declared on 298-4 and then removed openers Keaton Jennings and Marcus Harris before close to leave Lancashire needing 422 for victory.

Middlesex reached 184-4 in their second innings before close at Northwood and require 170 runs to win against Kent, who had made 254 all out.

articles.title: Australia thrash Bangladesh in second Test as Starc takes 10 wickets
articles.summary: Mitchell Starc takes 10 wickets in the match as Australia bounce back to win the second Test against Bangladesh by an innings and 51 runs and draw the series.
articles.body:
Bangladesh 64: Starc 6-12 & 95: Shanto 31; Starc 4-39, Cummins 3-10, Lyon 3-25

Mitchell Starc took 10 wickets in the match as Australia bounced back from last week's shock defeat by Bangladesh to win the second Test by an innings and 51 runs and draw the series 1-1.

The visitors were skittled for 95 in 38.3 overs with Starc taking four wickets and Nathan Lyon and captain Pat Cummins three each, as Australia wrapped up victory just after tea on the second day at the Great Barrier Reef Arena in Mackay.

Starc finished with match figures of 10-51, following his 6-12 in the first innings as Bangladesh struggled to 64 all out.

The game was the fourth-shortest completed Test match with a side winning, with exactly 125 overs bowled.

Last Sunday's nine-wicket defeat for the world's top-ranked side in Darwin was widely seen as one of Test cricket's greatest upsets.

"A lot of things went right these couple days and a lot of things went wrong last week," said Cummins, 33, who took 3-10 in the second innings.

"We needed to bounce back, and it was a great couple of days from the lads. I thought everyone was sharp. It was a great start and we didn't really let up after that."

Earlier in the day, Australia added 45 runs to their overnight total as they were bowled out for 210 with Cameron Green top scoring with 67 and Lyon adding an unbeaten 32 to give them a first-innings lead of 146.

Left-arm paceman Shoriful Islam was the pick of the bowlers with 7-48.

The visitors' second innings got off to a poor start, losing both openers inside eight overs as they slumped to 24-3.

They then collapsed in the middle session, struggling to 95-8 by tea before Lyon wrapped up victory by taking the final two wickets in three balls.

"Much better week. We knew we weren't at our best, or what we expect of ourselves, in Darwin," said 36-year-old Starc, who was named Player of the Match and Series after taking 12 wickets at an average of 12.08.

"What we expect of ourselves this week is what we got, particularly with the ball and the wicket that aided us with the ball."

Starc has now moved to 10th on the all-time Test wicket list with 445, 126 shy of Lyon's haul in sixth place.

Australia next Test series is a three-match tour of world Test champions South Africa in October.

articles.title: Australia hammer Bangladesh by an innings inside two days to tie Test series after shock opening loss
articles.summary: Bangladesh bowled out for 95 following first-innings 64 to lose by innings and 51 runs in Mackay; Australia left-arm pacer Mitchell Starc takes 10-for in match to finish series with 12 wickets at average of 12.08; series finishes tied at 1-1 after hosts' shock loss in Darwin opener
articles.body:
Australia responded to their shock opening loss to Bangladesh in Darwin with a thumping innings victory inside two days in Mackay to tie the two-Test series at 1-1.

Mitchell Starc took 4-39 to finish with match figures of 10-51 as Bangladesh ​were dismissed for less than 100 for the second time in the match.

Pat Cummins also claimed 3-10 and off-spinner Nathan Lyon 3-25 as Bangladesh were bowled out for 95 in 38.3 overs before tea on day two.

That followed their first-innings 64 all out, and though Australia themselves managed only a score of 210, that ultimately proved plenty as they wrapped up an innings-and-51-run victory.

  • Scorecard: Australia vs Bangladesh, second Test, Mackay
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract
  • Listen to episodes of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast

"Much better week," Starc, who was named Player of the Match, said. "We knew we weren't at our best, or what we expect of ourselves, in Darwin.

"What we expect of ourselves this week is what we got, particularly with the ball and the wicket that aided us with the ball."

As emphatic as the victory was, it may ​do little to ease concerns about Australia's batting before visiting reigning World Test Championship winners South ⁠Africa on a three-Test tour starting in October.

Australia, 165-8 overnight in their first innings, were evenutally bowled out ⁠for 210, with Cameron Green (67), who also scored a century in the first Test, the only batter to hit a half century.

The Tigers' recalled left-arm paceman Shoriful Islam took 7-48, for the best innings haul by a Bangladesh bowler in an away Test.

The visitors needed 146 runs to make the hosts ‌bat again but slumped to 39-3 by lunch and collapsed in the middle session, limping to 95-8 at tea.

Starc, who took a stunning 6-12 in the first innings, was Australia's chief destroyer with the ball again, the 36-year-old claiming 4-39.

He had opener Shadman Islam caught for one ‌before bowling Mominul Haque for a duck in his second over. He later had wicketkeeper Litton Das caught in the slips for a second successive duck and bowled tailender Taijul Islam for 11.

Already the most prolific left-arm pace bowler in Tests, Starc moved 10th on the all-time leading wicket-taker's list with 445 dismissals, four spots behind Lyon.

"Nathan (Lyon) didn't remind me that I've just stepped on the first rung of the ⁠ladder and he's still up there looking down on me," Starc said with a wry grin.

Lyon captured the key wicket of Bangladesh captain Najmul ​Hossain Shanto for 31, before taking the final two wickets in three balls straight after the tea break to wrap up ​the match.

articles.title: Rothesay County Championship: Somerset ramp up the pressure on Division One leaders Nottinghamshire
articles.summary: Somerset moved to within two points of the top of the table as they ramped up the pressure on County Championship Division One leaders Nottinghamshire; Kent keep up the pressure on leaders Durham in Division Two
articles.body:
Somerset ramped up the pressure on County Championship Division One leaders Nottinghamshire with an eight-wicket victory at home against Essex.

The home side required only 19.2 overs on day four to reach their target of 102, with Tom Lammonby finishing 39 not out, as they moved to within two points of the top of the table.

Essex put up resistance in their second innings but Jack Leach took 5-81 to finish with nine wickets in the game.

  • All today's County Championship scorecards
  • Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW

Lammonby and Josh Thomas, who got 31, made a stand of 59, but two wickets for Harmer were merely a consolation for Essex.

Struggling Leicestershire won for only the second time this season as they beat Glamorgan by 42 runs.

Kiran Carlson looked as though he might haul Glamorgan to victory with a promising 99 but after he fell to Ajaz Patel the visiting team's challenge faded.

For Leicestershire, Ian Holland took three wickets on day four, taking him to nine for the match, clinching things when last man Raymond Toole's wicket fell.

Hampshire remained bottom of the table after losing by 39 runs to Yorkshire.

In Division Two, Northamptonshire beat Lancashire by 316 runs at Old Trafford, with South African Ricardo Vasconcelos scoring a second-innings century before the hosts were skittled for 129 in 52.2 overs.

Kent kept up the pressure on leaders Durham as they won by 46 runs against Middlesex to move into second place.

A fine 144 by Dan Lategan helped Worcestershire to a comfortable eight-wicket over bottom side Gloucestershire, assisted by 107 not out from Jake Libby.

articles.title: Brydon Carse: What will it take to prevent England from more hangovers
articles.summary: Yet again, England are dealing with a player involved in a late-night incident. Only strong action will ensure there are no more, writes Stephan Shemilt.
articles.body:
Yet again, the England men's cricket team is picking through the wreckage of a late-night misdemeanour.

The latest stain on the game's reputation is a result of pictures of fast bowler Brydon Carse in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers outside a nightspot in Derby. His Durham team-mate Matthew Potts is in the images, while former England captain Ben Stokes appears in the background.

If you're keeping score, we're now up to eight England players involved in incidents of this kind since Halloween last year.

Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington, with Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue present. Ben Duckett was filmed drunk in Noosa, then Stokes and Gus Atkinson were there when a member of England's security staff was struck in a London nightclub in June, breaching a curfew in the process.

To put it another way, there are 30 men currently on England central contracts. More than a quarter of them have been caught up in bother in the past 10 months. Of the four separate incidents, two have involved punches being thrown and another was a police matter.

In Carse's case, the time spent in handcuffs came days after new England Test captain Joe Root called on his players to be "really good role models, good human beings".

Root was speaking the day before England's first Test against Pakistan, for which Carse was part of the squad. The match was scheduled to still be ongoing when he found himself in the hands of the police.

It is understood that Carse was not arrested. Both the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) and the Cricket Regulator will work to establish what happened. There are early suggestions he was denied entry back into a nightclub, or he had a drink poured over him.

Carse was also not specifically on England duty at the time. He was released from the first-Test squad to play for Durham away at Derbyshire and was scheduled to report to Lord's for the second Test on Monday.

As of Sunday evening, he remains part of the squad for the second Test. England will take time to gather some information before a decision on his involvement is made.

Root warned his squad to "be adults" when he abolished the midnight curfew - in his first act as captain - that came into place after previous incidents. As part of that move, guidelines advising players about not drinking alcohol on the day before, during or after a game, or in public, have also been removed.

There is a duty of care towards Carse. Two years ago, the 31-year-old was banned for historical betting offences and rebuilt his career to become an England regular in all three formats. No bowler has more Test wickets for England than Carse's 58 since he made his debut in October 2024.

But there is also a deep sense of anger and frustration within the ECB at having to deal with another error of judgement by a high-profile player. Supporters will take their own view, among them a sense that the behaviour of these players is now beyond parody.

Does someone have to be left out of a squad or given a meaty suspension for the penny to drop? This might be the opportunity for Root to stamp his authority on a new era.

Naturally, there will once again be the debate about not denying players their freedom or stopping them from enjoying a victory.

For Carse, a Saturday night out came less than 48 hours before he is scheduled to report for England. He is only a tweaked hamstring away from playing in a Test at Lord's on Thursday.

Perhaps more damning is the kind of trouble this group of England players seem to find. Two punch-ups and a set of handcuffs. It also does not appear to have dawned on them that they are high-profile individuals, likely to attract attention, with footage finding its way to social media, as happened with Carse.

And what about Stokes, who, despite being retired, remains an employee of the ECB via his central contract.

As the former captain, should Stokes have been conscious about Carse being in that situation? What about the trouble in which Atkinson found himself alongside Stokes in June?

Three weeks ago, Stokes denied the England team has a drinking culture, but rather that the game itself has a problem. What has Stokes done to distance himself or those around him from that drinking culture?

Now there is a wait to see what happens next. The ECB only became aware of the incident on Sunday afternoon. The governing body will take a breath overnight and decide if Carse needs to be removed from the Test squad.

Perhaps, on Tuesday, director of cricket Rob Key will once again explain why the players he manages cannot keep themselves out of trouble. In the aftermath of the Stokes-Atkinson incident in June, Key denied that England have become a "national embarrassment". He may be asked again.

Key also might be asked about the whereabouts of new Test coach Stephen Fleming, who does not take up his post until the winter. Might Carse have been less inclined to step out of line had the new sheriff been in town?

Well, here is another situation for England to manage. Only strong action will ensure there are no more.

articles.title: What has gone wrong for Pakistan cricket? Woes assessed after defeat to England in first Test at Headingley
articles.summary: Cricinfo senior editor Osman Samiuddin looks at reasons for Pakistan's toils in Test cricket with side having lost 14 of their last 19 matches; structure, administration and player management under the microscope; watch second England vs Pakistan Test live on Sky Sports from Thursday
articles.body:
It must be hard being a Pakistan cricket fan right now.

Those supporters have seen the side suffer 14 defeats in their last 19 Tests after last week's three-day, innings-and-103-run drubbing by England in the series opener at Headingley.

The tourists were loose and ineffective with the ball, poor with the bat and awful in the field - a damaging cocktail.

  • England romp to three-day win on Joe Root's captaincy return
  • England player ratings: Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue star
  • Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract

Ahead of the second game at Lord's from Thursday - live on Sky Sports Cricket (10am on air, 11am first ball) - Osman Samiuddin, a senior editor at Cricinfo and Pakistan cricket expert, joined Michael Atherton and Nasser Hussain on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast.

Samiuddin explained where he thinks things have gone wrong for Pakistan as cricket in the country reaches an "alarm bells stage" with fans "fed up" at how the game is being run…

Too much change with domestic structure

OSMAN SAYS: "Whichever structure you choose - there has been a great battle in Pakistan over the last 50 years, really, about whether you should have departmental or regional sides - I would pick one and stick with it, say this structure stays for the next 10, 12 years.

"They have changed structure almost every single season since the first first-class season in 1953. There has been no stability.

"We cut from 16 to six teams in 2019-20, then expanded to 16 teams with four first-class tournaments and three white-ball tournaments.

"When they cut down in 2019, they literally lost half their first-class cricketer pool. There were stories of players taking up driving taxis as, overnight, they didn't have a career.

"That drastic change every season has impacted the quality of domestic cricket, which is where you get your talent from.

"Domestic tournaments used to be played across 16 first-class grounds. For the last few years, they have been at about four or five.

"How are batters like Abdullah Shafique and Imam-ul-Haq supposed to work out how to play in different conditions playing at four grounds?"

Issues with administration and management of players

OSMAN SAYS: "A lot of it is self-inflicted.

"Since 2021, we have had four chairmen - Ramiz Raja, Najam Sethi, Zaka Ashraf and now Mohsin Naqvi - with very different views and very different levels of involvement in the game.

"The current chairman is also the interior minister of the country. Pakistan has a lot of interior-minister issues on any given day so he is fairly busy with his day job. You wonder how much time he has for cricket?

"Shaheen Shah Afridi, Babar Azam, Abdullah Shafique, Naseem Shah...

"So many of these players have burst onto the scene and then regressed. There is a feeling that golden talents have not hit the heights we are expecting them to hit and maybe never will.

"There is only one reason, really, for that regression and that is how the PCB manages their careers.

"They haven't managed them well enough whether through injury or basic player development stuff. There has been a succession of managements that haven't brought their best players on.

"There is no reason Shaheen and Naseem should not be leading Pakistan's pace attack but Naseem has not played a Test since December 2024 and Shaheen has played nine of 27 Tests since coming back from a knee injury.

"Shaheen injured his knee in a Test in Sri Lanka in 2022 fielding. There was a lot of confusion over the rehab and he was maybe rushed back.

"He has been hit by constant changes in the coaching set-up, never knowing who his coach is, who the bowling coach is, for example.

"He has hardly played a first-class game in three years and a fast bowler, you would think, would need to keep bowling to build your body up. Same for Naseem.

"What has become acute over the last five, six years is how wasteful Pakistan is of its talent. There has always been a certain amount of waste - it is not efficient - but that waste has increased more and more rapidly."

Samiuddin also noted how Naseem and Shaheen - not part of this Test squad - have been unceremoniously dropped at times without explanation, saying that "messes with a player's career."

Can fans be won back?

It was noticeable in Leeds how sparse the Pakistan support was and Samiuddin says patience with the governance is wearing thin.

He added: "I have heard more from fans anecdotally, not that they are angry at the team or because they are losing, but that they are fed up with how Pakistan cricket is being run. I suspect people will still turn up at Lord's to watch them.

paragraphs:
It must be hard being a Pakistan cricket fan right now.

Those supporters have seen the side suffer 14 defeats in their last 19 Tests after last week's three-day, innings-and-103-run drubbing by England in the series opener at Headingley.

The tourists were loose and ineffective with the ball, poor with the bat and awful in the field - a damaging cocktail.

Ahead of the second game at Lord's from Thursday - live on Sky Sports Cricket (10am on air, 11am first ball) - Osman Samiuddin, a senior editor at Cricinfo and Pakistan cricket expert, joined Michael Atherton and Nasser Hussain on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast.

Samiuddin explained where he thinks things have gone wrong for Pakistan as cricket in the country reaches an "alarm bells stage" with fans "fed up" at how the game is being run…

Too much change with domestic structure

OSMAN SAYS: "Whichever structure you choose - there has been a great battle in Pakistan over the last 50 years, really, about whether you should have departmental or regional sides - I would pick one and stick with it, say this structure stays for the next 10, 12 years.

"They have changed structure almost every single season since the first first-class season in 1953. There has been no stability.

"We cut from 16 to six teams in 2019-20, then expanded to 16 teams with four first-class tournaments and three white-ball tournaments.

"When they cut down in 2019, they literally lost half their first-class cricketer pool. There were stories of players taking up driving taxis as, overnight, they didn't have a career.

"That drastic change every season has impacted the quality of domestic cricket, which is where you get your talent from.

"Domestic tournaments used to be played across 16 first-class grounds. For the last few years, they have been at about four or five.

"How are batters like Abdullah Shafique and Imam-ul-Haq supposed to work out how to play in different conditions playing at four grounds?"

Issues with administration and management of players

OSMAN SAYS: "A lot of it is self-inflicted.

"Since 2021, we have had four chairmen - Ramiz Raja, Najam Sethi, Zaka Ashraf and now Mohsin Naqvi - with very different views and very different levels of involvement in the game.

"The current chairman is also the interior minister of the country. Pakistan has a lot of interior-minister issues on any given day so he is fairly busy with his day job. You wonder how much time he has for cricket?

"Shaheen Shah Afridi, Babar Azam, Abdullah Shafique, Naseem Shah...

"So many of these players have burst onto the scene and then regressed. There is a feeling that golden talents have not hit the heights we are expecting them to hit and maybe never will.

"There is only one reason, really, for that regression and that is how the PCB manages their careers.

"They haven't managed them well enough whether through injury or basic player development stuff. There has been a succession of managements that haven't brought their best players on.

"There is no reason Shaheen and Naseem should not be leading Pakistan's pace attack but Naseem has not played a Test since December 2024 and Shaheen has played nine of 27 Tests since coming back from a knee injury.

"Shaheen injured his knee in a Test in Sri Lanka in 2022 fielding. There was a lot of confusion over the rehab and he was maybe rushed back.

"He has been hit by constant changes in the coaching set-up, never knowing who his coach is, who the bowling coach is, for example.

"He has hardly played a first-class game in three years and a fast bowler, you would think, would need to keep bowling to build your body up. Same for Naseem.

"What has become acute over the last five, six years is how wasteful Pakistan is of its talent. There has always been a certain amount of waste - it is not efficient - but that waste has increased more and more rapidly."

Samiuddin also noted how Naseem and Shaheen - not part of this Test squad - have been unceremoniously dropped at times without explanation, saying that "messes with a player's career."

articles.title: Brydon Carse to miss England's second Test vs Pakistan as Cricket Regulator conducts investigation into nightclub incident
articles.summary: Video footage emerged of handcuffed Carse being led away by police on Saturday night; fast bowler had been out celebrating victory for Durham in County Championship after being released by England to play in game; Sonny Baker replaces Carse in squad for Lord’s Test from Thursday
articles.body:
England fast bowler Brydon Carse has been withdrawn from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's from Thursday following an incident outside a Derby nightclub that is being investigated by the Cricket Regulator.

Video footage emerged of a handcuffed Carse being led away by police on Saturday night after Durham's players had gone out to celebrate their win at Derbyshire in the County Championship.

Carse was seen talking to team-mate Matthew Potts with former England captain Ben Stokes also pictured in the background.

A Derbyshire Police statement read: "A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night (August 22).

"However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area."

An ECB statement read: "Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby.

"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Rothesay Test match while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."

Sonny Baker - who made his Test debut against New Zealand at The Kia Oval in June - replaces fellow seamer Carse in England's squad.

The Carse situation comes less than two weeks after new England captain Joe Root removed the midnight curfew that had been installed following a number of drink-related issues across the winter tours of New Zealand and Australia.

Carse did not make the England XI for the thumping three-day win over Pakistan in the series-opening Test at Headingley and was subsequently released to play for Durham against Derbyshire, a game in which he took two wickets and scored 26 runs.

Carse was England's leading wicket-taker during their 4-1 Ashes hammering but has not played for his country since due to injury.

Another off-field issue for England to manage

The paceman's nightclub incident is another off-field episode for England to negotiate.

White-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer while out the evening before a one-day international in New Zealand last autumn.

Then, during The Ashes, an unverified video appeared to show batter Ben Duckett drunk while the team were on a mid-series break in the beach resort of Noosa.

Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson missed the second Test of the 2-1 home defeat to New Zealand earlier this summer after breaking the curfew to attend a Chelsea nightclub as they celebrated victory in the first game of the series at Lord's.

Stokes and Atkinson were cleared of violent conduct but hit with written warnings after "breaching specific contractual obligations".

Root had called for his players to "be adults" while announcing the removal of the curfew, so the Carse situation will raise further questions about the side's relationship with alcohol.

Broad: Carse 'pretty daft' to be caught up in nightclub incident

Speaking on his For the Love of Cricket podcast, before Carse's withdrawal from the squad for the second Test was announced, former England bowler turned Sky Sports pundit Stuart Broad said: "We can't really make a judgement apart from it being, whatever's happened, pretty daft.

"We'll wait and see. We don't know, it could have been 10 o'clock in the evening, it could have been two o'clock, but whatever.

"This is not really anything that anybody wants to be talking about any more, to be brutally honest."

articles.title: Prasidh Krishna reveals his definition of aggression: 'It's about what I'm doing'
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: Every fast bowler has his own way of showing aggression. Some try to unsettle batters with eye contact, some stay calm, others rely on york.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Every fast bowler has his own way of showing aggression. Some try to unsettle batters with eye contact, some stay calm, others rely on yorkers, constant appeals or words. India pacer Prasidh Krishna has a different approach - he believes his aggression is best shown through his bowling.Krishna credited disciplined bowling, strong fielding and an attacking mindset for Indiaâs early success against Sri Lanka. The hosts were reduced to 8/2 before bad light ended Day Two of the second Test at the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground on Monday. India had declared on 503/9 after centuries from Devdutt Padikkal and Dhruv Jurel.The bowlers had only a short window to work with, but Krishna made it count, picking up a wicket with just his second delivery of the second over.âAggression can come out in different waysâKrishna said aggression is not necessarily about showing emotion or getting into a verbal battle with the opposition.âYeah, I would like to say so. I mean, aggression can come out in different ways, and for me it is about what I'm doing when I'm bowling. It's very easy for people to get away or be distracted by what's happening in the pitch. There's too much happening, there's not too much happening, but I think the focus is still to come in and bowl those areas with full effort,â Krishna told the broadcasters before the start of Day 3âs play.Krishna lauds JaiswalKrishna bowled back of a length outside off and found enough movement from the surface to trouble Lahiru Udara. The Sri Lankan opener edged towards gully, where Yashasvi Jaiswal completed an excellent diving catch to dismiss him for one.Krishna said the wicket was a result of both the conditions and Jaiswalâs fielding effort.âYeah, I think it was, thereâs something in the pitch, of course. Maybe stopped a little bit. There was a bit of seam, and I think credit goes to Jaiswal for the catch that he took. It was an exceptional one. We have been putting in some effort on the field in practice, so I think it just paid off,â he mentioned.â50% of the job is taking itâIndia had very little time to bowl before bad light stopped play. Manav Suthar then dismissed Prabath Jayasuriya for two with the final delivery of the day, leaving Sri Lanka at 8/2.Krishna stressed that creating chances is only half the job and the fielders also need to complete the opportunity.â100%. I think 50% of the job is bowling the ball there, getting an edge, but 50% is taking it as well, and we have been pretty good at doing that. I think it's also doing the simple things right, which we have been doing well, and that's what shows,â he added.Bowling to the conditionsKrishna also spoke about the need to adjust his length according to the pitch. He said the Indian coaching and analysis staff work together to decide the right approach for each surface.âLength is something that keeps changing with pitches that we play on. So we sit with analysts, coaches, and everything and decide on what's the kind of length that we want to be bowling on different surfaces. And yeah, natural length was something that I could say when I was not playing for the country, but when I'm here I need to be bowling every length that the team wants, and I'm trying to do that,â he concluded.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'They've fallen behind a little bit': Rahul Dravid on Team India's WTC final hopes
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: Former India head coach Rahul Dravid believes India still have a chance of reaching the World Test Championship final, but their path has b.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former India head coach Rahul Dravid believes India still have a chance of reaching the World Test Championship final, but their path has become tougher. India have slipped behind in the race and will need strong results in their remaining matches to make the top two.India are currently fifth in the WTC points table and face a difficult away series against New Zealand before hosting Australia in a five-Test series from January 2027.India have made a strong start to their ongoing series in Sri Lanka, leading 1-0 after winning the first Test in Galle by 165 runs. They have also taken control of the second Test after a big batting effort.Dravid feels the Sri Lanka series is an important first step, but India still have plenty of work to do."I'm hoping they do. It'll be a great run if India can qualify for the WTC final from here," Dravid told 'JioStar' when asked if India would be able to make the summit clash from here."They've fallen behind a little bit, but the kind of quality that the Indian team has, you're not going to write them off at any stage. They started off well against Sri Lanka, so that's a good first step," he said.New Zealand challenge awaitsIndia will travel to New Zealand in October for two Tests.Dravid expects the series to be a major test, especially for the younger players who have limited experience of playing in those conditions."(Playing against) New Zealand away, (is) always a challenge. (They are a) tough team, New Zealand, to play away from home. A lot of the young Indian boys have not played in those conditions, so that's going to be a big challenge," he said.Dravid also pointed out that India will miss the experience of several senior players who are no longer part of the Test side."Hopefully, they can keep the guys fit and not have a lot of injuries over the next few months. We're missing the experience of Virat (Kohli) and Rohit (Sharma), Ajinkya Rahane and (Cheteshwar) Pujara, these kinds of guys who've probably been there the last time India went. So that will be an interesting series as well," Dravid added.Australia series another big testAfter New Zealand, India will host Australia in a five-Test Border-Gavaskar Trophy series from January 2027. Dravid expects the Australian players to be highly motivated after failing to win a Test series in India in recent years."Australia will be really exciting. A lot of their players will be very keen to do well in India. That's a generation of truly great Australian players, a great Australian team that has not won in India. So they'll be keen to do that," Dravid said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
